newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova's three top leaders vie for presidency.
newsitem.headline: Moldova's three top leaders vie for presidency.

text.p: Moldova's president, prime minister and head of parliament have emerged as front-runners for a presidential election on Sunday in which relations with big regional power Russia are a key issue.

Relations with neighbouring Romania and a dispute with Slav rebels in Moldova's Dnestr region also figure large in campaigning by President Mircea Snegur, Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli and Parliament Chairman Petru Lucinschi.

None of the three, who lead a field of nine, is expected to garner more than half the votes in the first round -- required for an outright win in the former Soviet republic's first multi-party presidential ballot.
A run-off is on the cards for December 1 between the top two contenders, political analysts say.

The three front-runners hold differing views on future relations with big-power Russia -- prime provider of fuel for the landlocked, flat country of 4.3 million people, many of whom are desperately poor.
The next president will also have to try to press forward with economic recovery and stabilisation, which has won praise from the International Monetary Fund.
Of the three leading candidates, Sangheli, 52, wants the closest relations with Moscow -- particularly in view of the huge reliance of Moldova's large agricultural sector on Russian energy supplies.
He has cultivated the image of a man of few words who cares more about heating and power supplies than politics.
Centre-right Snegur, 56, elected in a single-candidate poll in December 1991, favours closer ties with Romania whose people share a common language, history and culture with Moldova.
Snegur wants to broaden his largely ceremonial powers, create a presidential republic and oust Sangheli's government dominated by the prime minister's Agrarian Party.

Relations with Romania overlap onto the Dnestr dispute where the mainly-Slav industrial region has said it will not allow Moldovan polling stations and insists it will elect its own president on December 22.
But local residents can vote outside the rebel region.
An eastern region with a population of 700,000, Dnestr broke away in 1990 fearing its mostly Slav residents would become second-class citizens if Moldova merged with Romania.
Hundreds of people died in fighting between Moldovan security forces and Dnestr rebels in March 1992 before a ceasefire was agreed in August 1992.

Since then negotiations mediated by Russia, Ukraine and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, have been blocked by disagreement over Dnestr's demands for statehood, although Moldova is offering it broad autonomy.
Snegur, though backed among others by nationalists, says Moldova should remain an independent state but his views on relations with Romania have irked Sangheli.
Last year Sangheli led opposition by his Agrarians to Snegur's proposal to rename the Moldovan language Romanian.
Lucinschi, 56, a left-leaning candidate running on an independent ticket, says his political credo is European-style social democracy and is backed by a number of leftist parties.

Standing somehwere between the two other contenders on the issue of relations with Russia and Romania, he says Moldova should have equally good relations with the East and the West. But he says ties with Russia are a priority.
"Our energy base is in Moscow, and the best market for our goods is also in Moscow," he said in a campaign booklet.
Unlike Sangheli, Lucinschi does not hesitate to call Romanians brothers, but talks mostly about economic ties.
